title: Moral and Spiritual Hunger in the Classroom
author: David Henreckson
summary: Henreckson argues that classrooms, like all human spaces, involve hunger—not just for knowledge but for meaning, transcendence, and purpose. Students bring this hunger whether or not teachers acknowledge it. Many schools, having secularized, present learning as instrumental (job preparation, standardized test scores) or as knowledge for its own sake. But this leaves the hunger unsatisfied. Students seeking purpose in a classroom devoted to function will find it elsewhere—in ideology, tribalism, charisma, or despair. The article contends that good teaching addresses this hunger not by imposing a particular worldview but by creating space for questions of meaning and value. Great teachers do this: they show why a subject matters, how it connects to human flourishing, what it reveals about our condition. They teach that learning is not just acquiring skills but developing the capacity to live well. The reframe is practical: in teaching history, a teacher can focus on dates and events, or on how people have grappled with justice, loss, and meaning. In literature, a teacher can focus on plot and technique, or on how stories reveal truth about being human. In science, a teacher can focus on facts and procedures, or on how understanding our world deepens wonder and responsibility. This shift does not require importing religion into schools; it requires acknowledging that meaning-making is part of learning. When students feel that a teacher cares about their growth as people—not just their test scores—something fundamental shifts. The classroom becomes a place where intellectual and spiritual hunger can both be addressed.

Schools that present learning as only instrumental (job prep) or abstract (knowledge for its own sake) leave this hunger unsatisfied, and students find meaning elsewhere.
Great teachers address hunger for meaning not by imposing ideology but by showing why subjects matter and how they connect to human flourishing.
Teaching meaning-making does not require importing religion; it requires acknowledging that learning is about developing the capacity to live well, not just acquiring skills.
When students feel teachers care about their growth as people—not just test scores—intellectual and spiritual hunger can both be addressed.
